current.role: First author of a 2014 mouse and cell study showing that the clock protein BMAL1 restrains mTORC1 and affects ageing.
current.sub: Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Diseases, Cleveland State University, Ohio
story: Rohini V. Khapre is first author of an Atlas study (KHA2014) on the circadian clock and ageing. Mice and cells lacking the clock protein BMAL1 had higher mTORC1 activity. Treating Bmal1 knockout mice with rapamycin raised their lifespan by 50 percent, which suggests BMAL1 normally acts as a brake on mTORC1. PubMed lists Khapre at the Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Diseases, Cleveland State University.

highlights.KHA2014: First author: reported that BMAL1 deficiency raises mTORC1 activity and that rapamycin lengthens life in Bmal1 knockout mice.

pubmed_affiliation: Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Diseases, BGES, Cleveland State University, Cleveland, OH.

studies.title: BMAL1-dependent regulation of the mTOR signaling pathway delays aging
studies.finding: Loss of the clock protein BMAL1 raised mTORC1 activity in mice and in cultured cells, and rapamycin extended the lifespan of Bmal1-/- mice by 50%. Places the circadian clock upstream of mTORC1 as a brake, and links that brake to ageing.

current.sub: Center for Molecular Medicine, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, NIH
story: J Julie Wu was first author of the Atlas study WUX2013 in Cell Reports. The mice carried a hypomorphic mTOR gene, so they made only about a quarter of the normal amount of mTOR. These mice lived longer and aged more slowly, but the slowing varied from tissue to tissue. It is a mouse study. PubMed lists Wu at the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute in Bethesda.

highlights.WUX2013: First author: showed that mice with reduced mTOR expression live longer, with tissue-specific slowing of aging.

pubmed_affiliation: Center for Molecular Medicine, National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD 20892, USA.

studies.title: Increased mammalian lifespan and a segmental and tissue-specific slowing of aging after genetic reduction of mTOR expression

current.lab_name: Center for Regenerative Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
current.role: First author of a 2021 mouse study imaging mTORC1 activity in acute myeloid leukemia.
current.sub: Center for Regenerative Medicine · Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, USA
story: Using fluorescent probes in the bone marrow of living mice, the study followed mTORC1 activity in leukemia cells. Activity fell as the disease advanced but was high at the moment of the best response to chemotherapy, where it was switched on rather than selected for. Blocking mTORC1 at that point killed more leukemia cells. Oki is the first of twelve authors, and PubMed lists the Center for Regenerative Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital.

highlights.OKI2021: First of twelve authors on the mouse imaging study of mTORC1 timing in acute myeloid leukemia.

pubmed_affiliation: Center for Regenerative Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, 02114, USA.

studies.title: Imaging dynamic mTORC1 pathway activity in vivo reveals marked shifts that support time-specific inhibitor therapy in AML
studies.finding: Fluorescent probes imaged in the bone marrow of live mice show mTORC1 activity in AML cells falls as the disease progresses but is high at the moment of maximal chemotherapy response, where it is induced rather than selected; inhibiting mTORC1 at that time improved killing of AML cells.

story: In ABD2026 (2026), Parveez Ahamed Abdul-Azees is the first author; the paper is a study in marmosets, a small primate, that found age-related loss of gland tissue and more fibrosis in the submandibular salivary gland, and that long-term oral rapamycin was associated with partly preserved gland structure and less fibrosis. PubMed lists the affiliation as: Center for Regenerative Sciences, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA.

highlights.ABD2026: First author of this paper, marmoset salivary gland aging.

pubmed_affiliation: Center for Regenerative Sciences, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA

studies.title: Rapamycin Attenuates Age-Related Changes in Marmoset Submandibular Gland: A Non-Human Primate Model of Human Oral Aging.
studies.finding:
In the aging marmoset submandibular gland the authors found fewer mucous and serous acinar units, expansion of ductal and collagen-rich stromal compartments, more extracellular matrix remodeling, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and more apoptotic and senescent cells. Chronic oral rapamycin was associated with partial preservation of acinar structure and with less fibrosis, lipid accumulation and fewer apoptotic and senescent cells, giving a tissue picture closer to that of younger animals.

current.lab_name: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science (Daejeon, South Korea)
current.role: First author of a 2026 mouse study showing that ectopic ERBB4 in excitatory neurons drives Alzheimer's-like changes through mTOR signalling.
current.sub: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science, and KAIST (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Se Young Lee was first author of a 2026 Nature paper in the Atlas (LEE2026), with 12 co-authors from IBS, KAIST and UNIST in Korea. In Alzheimer's disease mice, excitatory neurons switched on the gene Erbb4 early. Removing it protected against synapse loss, plaques and memory problems, and adding it to normal mice reproduced most of the damage, though not the plaques. These effects needed mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4.

highlights.LEE2026: First author; PubMed lists the author at the Center for Vascular Research of the Institute for Basic Science and in the Department of Biological Sciences at KAIST.

pubmed_affiliation: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science (IBS), Daejeon, Republic of Korea.

studies.title: Aberrant excitatory neuronal ERBB4 promotes Alzheimer's disease pathology
studies.finding: Ectopic ERBB4 in excitatory neurons is one of the earliest changes in AD mouse models and is necessary for synapse loss, reactive gliosis, amyloid plaque deposition and cognitive deficits in AD mice, and its overexpression in wild-type excitatory neurons is sufficient to reproduce synapse loss, gliosis and cognitive deficits (but not amyloid plaques); these effects require mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4.

story: Alex De Nardi is first author of a 2026 paper in the European Journal of Neurology. It is a secondary, retrospective analysis of data from RAP-ALS, a rapamycin trial in 63 people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The authors saw longer survival in the few treated people who carry a C9orf72 mutation. They call this exploratory because the group was small. PubMed lists him at COSBI in Rovereto and the Department of Mathematics at the University of Trento.

pubmed_affiliation: Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento Centre for Computational and Systems Biology (COSBI), Rovereto, Italy.

studies.title: Multivariate Survival Analysis of a Comprehensive Clinical Trial of Rapamycin in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Explores Prognostic Factors and Survival Patterns in C9orf72 Carriers
studies.finding: Secondary, observational survival analysis of the RAP-ALS rapamycin trial (n=63) finds a protective association between rapamycin treatment and survival in C9orf72 mutation carriers (log-rank p=0.026), consistent with a comparison against an independent C9orf72+ cohort (n=40; RMST p=0.04); confounding by indication is not excluded, and the authors flag this as exploratory given the small treated-carrier subgroup (n=6).

story: Stephen J. Simpson was last author of a 2014 mouse study in the Atlas, with Samantha M. Solon-Biet as first author. PubMed lists the author at the Charles Perkins Centre and the School of Biological Sciences of The University of Sydney.

Mice were fed many diets that varied in protein, fat and carbohydrate. Lifespan and metabolic health tracked the ratio of protein to carbohydrate, not total calories, and a low protein ratio went with lower mTOR activation in the liver.

highlights.SOL2014: Last author of the study linking the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio to lifespan, metabolic health and liver mTOR activation in mice.

pubmed_affiliation: Charles Perkins Centre, The University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, Australia

current.sub: Cochrane Institute of Primary Care and Public Health, School of Medicine, Cardiff University, Cardiff, UK
story: In BAN2014 (2014), Christian Bannister is the first author. The paper is a retrospective, observational study of UK patient records. People with type 2 diabetes who started metformin lived longer, on average, than matched people without diabetes. Because it is observational, patient selection and other confounders cannot be ruled out.
In the Atlas record PubMed gives the first name only as initials (C A). Two related papers from the same Cardiff group list him as Christian A Bannister with several of the same co-authors.

highlights.BAN2014: First author of this paper on metformin and survival in type 2 diabetes.

pubmed_affiliation: The Cochrane Institute of Primary Care and Public Health, School of Medicine, Cardiff University, Cardiff, UK

studies.title: Can people with type 2 diabetes live longer than those without? A comparison of mortality in people initiated with metformin or sulphonylurea monotherapy and matched, non-diabetic controls
studies.finding: Diabetic patients started on metformin had longer median survival than matched non-diabetic controls without the drug. Retrospective and observational: consistent with a survival benefit, but confounding by indication and healthy-adherer effects cannot be excluded.

story: Jiayuan Xie was first author of the Atlas study XIE2026 in Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety. In piglets and pig gut cells, bisphenol A damaged the jejunum (part of the small intestine) and its barrier. Glutamine in the diet eased the damage, along with better mitochondrial function and changes in AMPK-mTOR signalling. The paper suggests a link and does not prove the route. PubMed lists Xie at Shandong Agricultural University.

story: Kiryl Piatkevich was last author of the Atlas study WANG2026C in Science Advances. The team built a 'ticker tape' from self-assembling protein fibres and several colours of fluorescent protein, so that single living cells keep a record of past gene activity. Versions were made for several pathways, including mTOR. With the mTOR version they saw mTOR activity rise and fall with the cell cycle. PubMed lists Piatkevich at Zhejiang University and Westlake University in Hangzhou.

highlights.WANG2026C: Last author: senior author of the ticker tape tool used to see cell-cycle-dependent oscillations in mTOR activity.

pubmed_affiliation: College of Life Sciences, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China.

studies.title: Fluorescent protein ticker tape (FPTT): Multiplexed recording of transcriptional dynamics in living cells and in vivo
studies.finding: Engineered a multiplexed fluorescent-protein 'ticker tape' biosensor platform (self-assembling protein fibers + multispectral fluorescent proteins) for longitudinal, single-cell recording of signaling-pathway transcriptional histories (mTOR, NF-κB, STAT3, NFAT, cAMP). Applying the mTOR-FPTT reporter, the authors independently observed cell-cycle-dependent OSCILLATING mTOR activity dynamics -- a new, orthogonal tool corroborating that mTOR signaling is patterned over time rather than static, consistent with JOS2024's cell-cycle oscillation finding.

The paper reports that oxidative stress switches on a PI3K-AKT-mTORC1-eIF4A chain that quickly raises production of P-glycoprotein, a pump that expels drugs. This works by changing translation of the mRNA rather than by turning up the gene. PubMed lists Jin at the College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University.

highlights.JIN2026: First author: reported the redox-sensitive mTOR-eIF4A route that boosts P-glycoprotein translation.

pubmed_affiliation: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University, Chongqing, China.

studies.finding: Oxidative stress activates a redox-sensitive PI3K-AKT-mTORC1-eIF4A cascade that selectively promotes P-glycoprotein translation via cap-dependent mRNA engagement, revealing a transcription-independent mechanism of rapid multidrug resistance induction.

current.sub: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute & Department of Cell Biology · Harvard Medical School · Boston, MA, USA
story: John T Cunningham is first author of a 2007 paper in Nature. The study, done in cells, showed that mTORC1 helps run the cell's energy supply. It does this through a complex of YY1 and PGC-1alpha that switches on mitochondrial genes and raises oxygen use. Rapamycin lowered that mitochondrial output.
PubMed lists him at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Department of Cell Biology at Harvard Medical School in Boston.

highlights.CUN2007: First author of the study showing that mTOR controls mitochondrial oxidative function through a YY1-PGC-1alpha complex.

pubmed_affiliation: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts 02115, USA.

studies.title: mTOR controls mitochondrial oxidative function through a YY1-PGC-1alpha transcriptional complex
studies.finding: Showed mTOR isn't just about building proteins - it also runs the cell's POWER plants. mTORC1 drives mitochondrial gene expression and oxygen consumption through a YY1-PGC-1alpha transcriptional program; block mTOR with rapamycin and mitochondrial output falls. Explains part of why mTOR inhibition reshapes metabolism.

current.role: First author of a 2026 study on CASTOR1, an arginine sensor that restrains mTORC1 in B cells, and lupus-like disease in mice.
current.sub: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, University of Tokyo (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Takeshi Kusuda was first author of a 2026 Atlas study from the University of Tokyo (KUS2026). It gave the arginine sensor CASTOR1 a clear job upstream of mTORC1. Mice without it had more active mTORC1 in B cells, more antibody-making plasma cells, and lupus-like kidney damage. In people with lupus, lower CASTOR1 in plasmablasts went with higher disease activity.

highlights.KUS2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Allergy and Rheumatology at the University of Tokyo.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan.

studies.title: CASTOR1 regulates humoral immune responses and contributes to the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus
studies.finding: Gives the arginine sensor CASTOR1 a defined physiological job upstream of mTORC1: losing it de-represses mTORC1 in B cells and drives plasma-cell expansion, IgG and anti-dsDNA autoantibodies, and lupus-like glomerulonephritis. In human SLE, CASTOR1 expression in plasmablasts was inversely correlated with disease activity (r = -0.32, p = 0.00031). One of the few studies to tie a specific upstream amino-acid sensor to a human autoimmune phenotype rather than to cancer or growth.

current.lab_name: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Seoul, South Korea)
current.role: First author of the 2026 study of the D-leucine prodrug DLMEH, which activates mTORC1 through Sestrin2 in muscle atrophy models.
current.sub: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine, Seoul
story: Jae Ho Shim was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas on DLMEH, a modified D-leucine compound. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Anatomy of the Korea University College of Medicine in Seoul.

DLMEH bound Sestrin2 about as strongly as L-leucine and switched on mTORC1 in a Sestrin2-dependent way. It restored protein synthesis in human muscle cells and kept muscle mass, grip strength and endurance in rats with drug-induced muscle wasting. That rat model is not an ageing model of sarcopenia.

highlights.SHIM2026: First author of the study of DLMEH as a Sestrin2-dependent mTORC1 activator in muscle cells and rats.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea

studies.title: D-Amino Acid Prodrug DLMEH Activates mTORC1 via Sestrin2 to Restore Muscle Protein Synthesis in Sarcopenia.
studies.finding: DLMEH, a D-leucine ester prodrug, binds Sestrin2 with leucine-like potency (Kd 28.3 uM, equivalent to L-leucine) and activates mTORC1 in a Sestrin2-dependent way. It restored protein synthesis in human myotubes and preserved muscle mass, grip strength and endurance in a rat dexamethasone-induced atrophy model (not an ageing sarcopenia model).

current.role: Co-author of two studies on how lysosomal cholesterol feeds into mTORC1.
current.sub: Department of Anatomy, University of California San Francisco · listed on two Atlas papers, 2017 and 2022
story: Rushika M Perera is a middle author on two Science papers about cholesterol as a signal to mTORC1. PubMed lists her in the Department of Anatomy at the University of California, San Francisco, on both, while the first authors worked at UC Berkeley.

The 2017 paper showed that cholesterol in the lysosome activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9. The 2022 paper identified LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein that senses cholesterol and holds back the GATOR1 complex. Both were done in cultured cells.

highlights.CAS2017: Middle author of the study showing lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via SLC38A9 and NPC1.
highlights.SHI2022: Middle author of the study identifying LYCHOS as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Anatomy, University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, CA 94143, USA.

studies.title: Lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via an SLC38A9-Niemann-Pick C1 signaling complex
studies.finding: Establishes lysosomal cholesterol as a nutrient input that drives mTORC1 recruitment and activation at the lysosomal surface. SLC38A9 is required for cholesterol-driven mTORC1 activation through conserved cholesterol-responsive motifs, and does so independently of its arginine-sensing function; NPC1, which exports cholesterol from the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and restrains mTORC1 through its sterol transport function. Boundary: cell lines and patient-derived fibroblasts, no organismal endpoint.

studies.title: Lysosomal GPCR-like protein LYCHOS signals cholesterol sufficiency to mTORC1
studies.finding: Identifies LYCHOS (previously annotated GPR155) as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1. Cholesterol binds the amino-terminal permease-like region; mutating that site impairs mTORC1 activation. At high cholesterol LYCHOS binds GATOR1 through a conserved cytoplasm-facing loop, and by sequestering GATOR1 it promotes cholesterol- and Rag-dependent recruitment of mTORC1 to the lysosome. Boundary: human cell lines and biochemistry, not an organismal phenotype.

story: Jiafeng Yu was first author of the Atlas study YU2026 in Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry. In mice with sepsis-associated encephalopathy, mTOR was overactive in the prefrontal cortex, which held back oligodendrocyte maturation and myelin and led to memory problems. Inhaled hydrogen gas and rapamycin both lowered mTOR activity, restored myelination and improved cognition. It is a mouse study. PubMed lists Yu at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital.

highlights.YU2026: First author: reported that hydrogen gas restrains mTOR overactivation and improves cognition in septic mice.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, Tianjin 300052, PR China; Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology, Tianjin 300052, PR China.

studies.title: High-concentration hydrogen mitigates cognitive impairment in a murine model of Sepsis-associated encephalopathy by enhancing oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination in the mPFC
studies.journal: Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry
studies.finding: In a mouse model of sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE), mTOR hyperactivation impairs oligodendrocyte maturation and causes cognitive deficits; hydrogen gas and rapamycin suppress mTOR, restore myelination, and improve cognition in these mice.

current.lab_name: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital (Tianjin, China)
current.role: Last author of a mouse study of hydrogen gas, mTOR and myelination in sepsis-associated encephalopathy.
current.sub: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital · Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology
story: Yang Yu was last author of the Atlas study YU2026 in Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry. The mouse study found that mTOR hyperactivation in the prefrontal cortex impairs oligodendrocyte maturation and causes cognitive deficits after sepsis. Hydrogen gas and rapamycin suppressed mTOR, restored myelination and improved cognition. PubMed lists Yu at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital.

highlights.YU2026: Last author: senior author of the mouse study on hydrogen gas, mTOR and myelination.

story: Hani Goodarzi is a middle author on two Atlas papers with UCSF groups. The 2023 paper tested RMC-6272, a drug that blocks mTORC1 much more than mTORC2, and found it killed ER-positive breast cancer cells and overcame resistance to other therapies in cells and patient-derived tumours in mice (MEN2023). The 2026 paper showed that the dipeptide transporter SLC15A3 keeps mTORC1 active in lymphoma cells that resist antimetabolite chemotherapy, and that those resistant cells were sensitive to rapamycin (YAN2026).
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics at UCSF on both, and at the Arc Institute on the 2026 paper.

highlights.MEN2023: Middle author of the bi-steric mTORC1 inhibitor study in breast cancer.
highlights.YAN2026: Middle author of the SLC15A3 lymphoma study; PubMed also lists the author at the Arc Institute.

studies.title: A bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor overcomes drug resistance in breast cancer
studies.finding: RMC-6272, a bi-steric molecule with >25-fold selectivity for mTORC1 over mTORC2, completely suppresses mTORC1 (hitting the rapamycin-resistant substrate 4E-BP1) and overcomes hormone- and CDK4/6-inhibitor resistance in breast cancer cell lines and PDX -- the preclinical basis for the RMC-5552 selective-inhibitor clinical program.

studies.title: SLC15A3-mediated dipeptide metabolism confers antimetabolite resistance in lymphoma via mTORC1 activation.
studies.finding: SLC15A3-mediated dipeptide import sustains mTORC1 activation in B cell lymphomas, enabling resistance to antimetabolite chemotherapy. Silencing SLC15A3 lowered mTORC1 activity and restored sensitivity to 6-mercaptopurine, and the resistant lymphomas, but not the parental tumours, were selectively sensitive to rapamycin in culture and in vivo.
